# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 1 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalent)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 1

**1** The man who raised me sold me to a certain Rhoda in Rome. Many years later I came to recognize her, and I came to love her as a sister. **2** Sometime after this I saw her bathing in the Tiber River and I offered her my hand and brought her out of the river. When I observed her beauty I began to reason within my heart: "How happy I would be if I had a wife of such beauty and character." That is all I thought — nothing more. **3** After some time had passed, while I was journeying to Cumae and giving praise to God's creation — how magnificent, marvelous, and mighty it all is — as I was walking along, I fell into a trance. **4** The Spirit seized me and brought me away through a pathless region that no man could traverse; it was rugged country, full of gullies cut by waterways. **5** Having crossed over that river I reached level ground, knelt down, and began to pray to the Lord, confessing my sins. **6** While I was praying, the heavens opened, and I saw the woman I had desired greeting me from heaven, saying, "Greetings, Hermas." **7** I looked up at her and replied, "Lady, what are you doing here?" She answered me, "I have been taken up to accuse you of your sins before the Lord." **8** I said to her, "Are you now acting as my accuser?" "No," she said, "but hear the words I am about to speak to you. The God who dwells in the heavens — who created all that exists out of nothing and increased it and multiplied it for the sake of his holy church — **9** he is wrathful with you because you sinned against me." I answered and said, "How have I sinned against you? In what respect? When did I ever say a shameful word to you? Have I not always treated you with the respect due a goddess? Have I not always honored you with the respect due a sister? Why then, woman, do you falsely charge me with these foul and impure things?" **10** She laughed and said to me, "The desire for wickedness rose up in your heart. Do you not consider it sin for a righteous man to nurse an evil desire in his heart? Yes," she said, "it is sin, and a grievous one. For the righteous man sets his aim on righteous things. **11** So long as he aims at righteous things and walks accordingly, he has a Lord in the heavens. But those who aim at wickedness and walk in it have a lord who is wicked, ruinous, and destructive. They pass through life crushed between these two poles. **12** Indeed, whenever holy and righteous people entertain evil desires, they heap sin upon themselves."

---

*LOGOS note: "trance" renders the Greek ekstasis-adjacent sleep; "goddess" (thea) preserved as metaphor for deep reverence, not literal deity.*
